pages.title: What is Energy Conversion?
pages.body: Energy conversion is the process by which energy changes from one form into another form, without the total amount of energy being lost or gained overall. Chemical, electrical, heat, light, sound and kinetic energy are some of the common forms of energy studied in science, and in almost every device or activity around us, energy is being converted from one of these forms into another to do useful work.

questions.q: Energy conversion is best described as
o: Energy changing from one form into another
Energy staying in exactly the same form forever
questions.e: Energy conversion is the process by which energy changes from one form into another form, without the total amount of energy being lost or gained overall.

pages.title: Common Examples of Energy Conversion
pages.body:
Electric bulbs, burning fuels, moving vehicles, solar panels, batteries and even the human body are everyday examples where energy conversion takes place, as summarised in the table below.

| **DEVICE OR ACTIVITY** | **ENERGY CONVERSION** | **EVERYDAY EXAMPLE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Electric bulb** | Electrical energy to light and heat energy | A lamp lighting a room at night |
| **Burning wood or charcoal** | Chemical energy to heat and light energy | Cooking food over an open fire |
| **Moving vehicle** | Chemical energy (fuel) to kinetic energy | A car or motorbike travelling on a road |
| **Solar panel** | Light energy to electrical energy | Solar panels charging a phone or powering a home |
| **Dry cell battery** | Chemical energy to electrical energy | A torchlight or a remote control |
| **Human body** | Chemical energy (food) to kinetic and heat energy | Walking, running or lifting an object |

pages.title: Why Energy Conversion Matters
pages.body: Almost every useful activity carried out by machines, living things or natural processes depends on converting energy from a stored or less useful form into a more useful form for the task at hand. Without energy conversion, the chemical energy stored in food, fuel or batteries would remain locked away and unable to power movement, light, sound or heat, which are the forms of energy we actually rely on in daily life.

Notice that in each example, energy does not disappear. Instead, it changes form, often into more than one type at once. For example, an electric bulb converts electrical energy mainly into light energy, but also produces some heat energy as a side effect, which is why a bulb feels warm after being on for a while.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Scientists describe this idea using the law of conservation of energy, which states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another. This means that whenever energy conversion appears to produce less useful energy than expected, such as a car engine producing a lot of heat in addition to motion, the missing energy has not vanished. It has simply been converted into a form, often heat, that is not being put to useful work in that situation.

pages.title: Why Energy Conversion is Important
pages.body: Powering homes, running industries, supporting transport, and preserving natural resources are among the many reasons energy conversion is considered important in modern life. Since most of the energy found in nature, such as sunlight, moving water and wind, is not in a directly useful form for most human activities, energy conversion allows this natural energy to be transformed into forms such as electricity, which can then power lights, machines, and countless other devices people depend on daily.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How a Dammed River Produces Electricity

pages.title: How a Dammed River Produces Electricity
pages.body:
Storing water, releasing it to fall, turning a turbine, and driving a generator are the four main stages that describe how a dammed river is converted into a useful supply of electricity, known as hydroelectric power.

- First, a dam is built across a river, creating a large reservoir that stores water at a high level behind the dam wall.

- Second, this stored water is allowed to fall through a large pipe, called a penstock, gaining kinetic energy as it falls.

- Third, the fast moving, falling water strikes the blades of a turbine, causing it to spin rapidly.

- Fourth, the spinning turbine drives a generator, which converts this kinetic energy into electrical energy that is then sent out through transmission lines.

pages.title: Harnessing Other Natural Forms of Energy
pages.body:
Falling water, wind, sunlight, heat from beneath the earth, and biogas from waste are five natural sources of energy that can be harnessed and converted into more directly useful forms, as summarised in the table below.

| **NATURAL ENERGY SOURCE** | **HOW IT IS HARNESSED** | **FORM PRODUCED** |
|---|---|---|
| **Falling water (a dammed river)** | Water is stored behind a dam and released to fall through a turbine | Electrical energy |
| **Wind** | Moving air turns the blades of a wind turbine connected to a generator | Electrical energy |
| **Sunlight** | Solar panels made of photovoltaic cells capture sunlight directly | Electrical energy |
| **Heat from beneath the earth (geothermal)** | Steam from underground heat is used to turn turbines | Electrical energy |
| **Plant and animal waste (biogas)** | Waste is broken down by bacteria in an airtight tank to release gas | Gas used for heat or electrical energy |

In each case, a specific piece of technology, such as a turbine, solar panel, or biogas digester, is used to capture the natural energy source and convert it into a form, usually electricity or heat, that people can use directly in their homes, farms and industries.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Ghana relies significantly on hydroelectric power from dams such as the Akosombo Dam on the Volta River, which has supplied a large share of the country's electricity since it was built. Understanding how such dams work helps explain why prolonged periods of low rainfall can sometimes lead to reduced electricity generation, since less water is available to fall through the turbines, showing how closely energy conversion for electricity can be tied to natural conditions such as rainfall.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain renewable and nonrenewable sources of energy.
- Identify the various sources of renewable and nonrenewable forms of energy and classify them, for example wind, coal, hydro, crude oil, natural gas, solar and biogas.
- Describe how to produce energy from a renewable source.

pages.title: Renewable and Nonrenewable Energy Defined
pages.body:
Renewable and nonrenewable are the two broad categories used to classify all energy sources, based on how quickly nature can replace the source after it has been used. A renewable source of energy is one that is naturally replaced within a short period of time, so it will not run out even with continued use, such as sunlight, wind, moving water and biogas. A nonrenewable source of energy is one that took millions of years to form and is being used up far faster than nature can replace it, such as coal, crude oil and natural gas.

| **CATEGORY** | **SOURCES** | **KEY CHARACTERISTIC** |
|---|---|---|
| **Renewable** | Solar, wind, hydro (falling water) and biogas | Naturally replaced within a short time, so it will not run out with continued use |
| **Nonrenewable** | Coal, crude oil and natural gas | Formed over millions of years and used up much faster than nature can replace it |

pages.title: Classifying Energy Sources
pages.body:
Solar, wind, hydro, biogas, coal, crude oil, and natural gas are the seven common energy sources studied at this level, and each one can be classified as either renewable or nonrenewable, as shown below.

- Solar energy, from sunlight, is renewable, since the sun continues to shine every day.

- Wind energy, from moving air, is renewable, since wind patterns are continuously produced by natural weather processes.

- Hydro energy, from falling or flowing water, is renewable, since rainfall continues to refill rivers and reservoirs.

- Biogas, from the breakdown of plant and animal waste, is renewable, since waste continues to be produced as long as living things exist.

- Coal, crude oil and natural gas are all nonrenewable, since they formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals over millions of years and cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

pages.title: Producing Energy from a Renewable Source
pages.body: Capturing the natural energy, converting it into electricity or heat, and delivering it for use are the three general steps involved in producing energy from any renewable source. For example, to produce energy from solar power, sunlight is captured by solar panels made of photovoltaic cells, converted directly into electrical energy, and then delivered through wires to charge batteries or power appliances directly. Similarly, to produce energy from wind, moving air turns the blades of a wind turbine, which spins a generator to produce electricity that can then be used or stored.

Notice that renewable sources are generally tied to ongoing natural processes, such as sunlight, wind and rainfall, that continue indefinitely, while nonrenewable sources are tied to a fixed, limited stock that was formed long ago and does not renew itself within a human lifetime.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Although renewable energy sources do not run out in the same way nonrenewable sources do, they are not always available at every moment. For example, solar panels produce little electricity at night or during heavy cloud cover, and wind turbines produce little electricity on very calm days. This is why many renewable energy systems are often combined with batteries or connected to a wider electricity grid, so that energy can still be available even when the immediate natural source is temporarily weak.

pages.title: What Does Managing Renewable Energy Sustainably Mean?
pages.body: Managing renewable energy sustainably means using and maintaining renewable energy sources in a way that keeps them productive and reliable over the long term, without damaging the environment or the resource itself. Even though renewable sources such as sunlight, wind and water are naturally replenished, poor planning, poor maintenance, or overuse of related infrastructure can still reduce how effectively these sources are used.

questions.e: Managing renewable energy sustainably means using and maintaining renewable energy sources in a way that keeps them productive and reliable over the long term, without damaging the environment or the resource itself.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Stages Involved in Managing Renewable Energy Sources

pages.title: Stages Involved in Managing Renewable Energy Sources
pages.body:
Planning, installation, monitoring, maintenance and improvement are five general stages involved in the sustainable management of any renewable energy source.

- Planning involves assessing local conditions, such as sunlight hours, wind speed or rainfall patterns, to determine which renewable source is most suitable for a given location.

- Installation involves setting up the necessary equipment, such as solar panels, wind turbines, dam infrastructure or biogas digesters, correctly and safely.

- Monitoring involves regularly checking how much energy is being produced and identifying any problems early.

- Maintenance involves cleaning, repairing and replacing worn out parts to keep the system working efficiently.

- Improvement involves upgrading technology or expanding capacity over time as needs grow or better solutions become available.

pages.title: Challenges in Managing Renewable Energy Sources
pages.body:
Weather dependence, maintenance needs, and resource supply are common challenges that affect how reliably each renewable energy source can be managed, along with practical solutions communities can adopt, as shown in the table below.

| **RENEWABLE SOURCE** | **MANAGEMENT CHALLENGE** | **POSSIBLE SOLUTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Solar** | Produces little or no electricity at night or during heavy cloud cover | Store excess electricity in batteries during sunny periods for later use |
| **Wind** | Produces little electricity when wind speeds are very low | Combine with other energy sources or battery storage systems |
| **Hydro** | Depends on rainfall, so droughts can reduce water levels and electricity output | Manage reservoir levels carefully and combine with other energy sources |
| **Biogas** | Requires regular maintenance and a steady supply of organic waste | Establish a reliable waste collection and digester maintenance routine |

Notice that although each of these sources is naturally renewable, none of them manages itself automatically. Solar panels need regular cleaning to remove dust, wind turbines need regular servicing, dams need careful water level management, and biogas digesters need a steady, well managed supply of waste material.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Sustainable management of renewable energy also involves social and economic planning, not just technical maintenance. For example, communities need to be trained to operate and repair small scale renewable energy systems themselves, and the cost of maintaining equipment needs to be budgeted for over its full lifetime, not just at the time of installation, to avoid renewable energy projects failing after only a few years due to neglect.

pages.title: What is Heat?
pages.body: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter object or region to a colder one, as a result of a difference in temperature between them. Heat is measured in joules, the same unit used for other forms of energy, and the total amount of heat energy an object contains depends on both its temperature and its mass. For example, a large pot of warm water contains more heat energy than a small cup of water at the same temperature, simply because it has more mass.

questions.q: Heat is measured in
questions.e: Heat is measured in joules, the same unit used for other forms of energy, and the total amount of heat energy an object contains depends on both its temperature and its mass.

pages.title: What is Temperature?
pages.body: Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold an object is, based on the average movement of the tiny particles that make it up. Temperature is measured using a thermometer, usually in degrees Celsius, and unlike heat, temperature does not depend on the mass or amount of the substance. This is why a small cup of boiling water and a large pot of boiling water can have exactly the same temperature, even though the pot contains far more heat energy.

pages.title: Distinguishing Features of Heat and Temperature
pages.body:
Definition, unit of measurement, instrument used, and what each depends on are four useful features for distinguishing between heat and temperature, as summarised in the table below.

| **FEATURE** | **HEAT** | **TEMPERATURE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | A form of energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder object | A measure of how hot or cold an object is |
| **Unit of measurement** | Joules | Degrees Celsius or Kelvin |
| **Instrument used** | Calorimeter (in advanced studies) | Thermometer |
| **What it depends on** | The mass of the substance and how much energy it contains | Does not depend on the amount or mass of the substance |
| **Nature** | A form of energy | A measure or indicator of the level of heat energy present |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Relationship Between Heat and Temperature

pages.title: The Relationship Between Heat and Temperature
pages.body: Heat and temperature are closely related but are not the same thing. Heat is the energy itself, while temperature is a measure of the intensity or concentration of that heat energy within an object. When heat flows into an object, its temperature usually rises, since the particles gain energy and move faster. Conversely, when heat flows out of an object, its temperature usually falls. In the environment, this relationship explains why the sun heats the earth's surface during the day, raising its temperature, while the surface loses heat at night, causing its temperature to fall.

pages.title: Temperature Scales and Thermometers
pages.body:
On the Celsius scale pure ice melts at 0 degrees and pure water boils at 100 degrees at normal pressure. Scientists also use the Kelvin scale. To change a temperature from degrees Celsius to kelvin, add 273. So 0 degrees Celsius is 273 kelvin, the normal body temperature of 37 degrees Celsius is 310 kelvin and 100 degrees Celsius is 373 kelvin.

| **THERMOMETER** | **HOW IT WORKS** | **RANGE AND USE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid in glass laboratory thermometer** | Mercury or coloured alcohol in a bulb expands when heated and rises up a narrow tube | About 10 degrees below zero to 110 degrees Celsius. Used for experiments |
| **Clinical thermometer** | A narrow bend in the tube stops the liquid from falling back before the reading is taken | About 35 to 42 degrees Celsius. Used to measure body temperature |
| **Digital thermometer** | An electronic sensor measures the temperature and shows it as a number | Now widely used in clinics and homes because it is quick and safe |

questions.e: Temperature is measured using a thermometer, usually in degrees Celsius, and unlike heat, temperature does not depend on the mass or amount of the substance.

pages.title: How Heat is Transferred
pages.body:
| **METHOD** | **HOW HEAT MOVES** | **EXAMPLE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Conduction** | Heat passes from particle to particle through a material, mainly in solids | The handle of a metal spoon left in hot soup becomes hot |
| **Convection** | Heated liquid or gas becomes lighter and rises while cooler liquid or gas sinks, which sets up a current | Water circulating in a pot on a fire, and sea breezes |
| **Radiation** | Heat travels as rays and needs no material to travel through | Heat from the Sun reaching the Earth, and the warmth felt beside a fire |

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:i807005221|Fig 4.4  Particle movement at low and high temperature]]

Notice that at a higher temperature, the particles move faster and with more energy, while at a lower temperature, the particles move more slowly. Temperature is essentially a measure of this average particle movement, while heat is the actual energy transferred as a result of a temperature difference between two objects or regions.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

A helpful way to remember the difference is that temperature tells you how hot something feels, while heat tells you how much total thermal energy is involved in changing that temperature. This is why it takes far more heat energy to raise the temperature of a swimming pool by one degree than to raise the temperature of a cup of water by the same one degree, even though the temperature change is identical in both cases.
